strengths: The problem is practically relevant: anonymizing stored video embeddings while keeping a large encoder frozen could reduce the cost of privacy-aware downstream analysis.

The utility evaluation is broad, covering action recognition, temporal action detection, and anomaly detection across multiple encoder families. Table 1 shows substantial reductions in measured VISPR predictability with small utility losses.
The ablations provide useful evidence for latent consistency. In Table 5, it improves unseen-task THUMOS14 mAP from 3.81 to 56.50 while retaining action-recognition performance.

The appendix includes architecture, optimization, runtime, and precomputed-feature experiments. The gender-bias experiments also show improvements in disadvantaged-group accuracy alongside smaller aggregate performance gaps.
weaknesses: The privacy evidence does not adequately establish the central anonymization claim. VISPR evaluates seven attributes on repeated-frame static clips, whereas deployment releases representations of real videos. Section 4.1 specifies a linear attacker, while Appendix B specifies a two-layer MLP, leaving the evaluated threat model inconsistent. There is no systematic attacker-capacity sweep, adaptive recovery evaluation, or multi-clip attack. PA-HMDB provides some video-domain evidence, but privacy cMAP only decreases from 69.9 to 62.6, and its attacker protocol is insufficiently specified.

The interpretation of the privacy objective is technically overstated. Maximizing a fixed cosine-based NT-Xent loss does not establish minimization of mutual information: weakening a contrastive lower bound does not upper-bound the information remaining in the representation. Reduced similarity could reflect an altered representation geometry rather than removal of sensitive information. The claims that the method destroys mutual information and removes all unnecessary spatial information need substantially stronger justification.

Novelty and comparative evaluation are incomplete. The components largely combine an existing reversed contrastive objective, a standard attention adapter, multitask learning, and feature reconstruction. Related work does not adequately position this combination against latent representation sanitization and adversarial attribute removal. Comparisons primarily target pixel-space methods on I3D; matched latent-space baselines and comparable privacy–utility curves on foundation models are missing.

Unseen-task generalization is weaker than the headline claims suggest. Table 1 uses training on all three utility tasks. With action-recognition-only training, THUMOS14 drops from 60.82 to 56.45; Toyota-trained anonymization reduces it to 41.30 and UCF-Crime AUC from 85.79 to 74.92. Table 12 also shows substantial detection losses. The approximately 35% privacy reduction is not consistent across backbones, and near-baseline utility should be distinguished from generalization to held-out tasks.

The fairness evidence is preliminary. NTU results use one shortcut action, and Toyota results report aggregate gender-group accuracy gaps without controlling for different action distributions. There are no dedicated debiasing baselines, repeated shortcut selections, or uncertainty estimates. These experiments support improved group performance in the tested settings but do not establish broad mitigation of gender bias.

Reproducibility and statistical reliability need improvement. The temporal token organization supplied to AAM, multitask sampling schedule, and several evaluation split details are insufficiently specified. No seed variability or confidence intervals are reported, despite some small gains. Reported values also differ without explanation, including the raw HMDB51 baseline in Tables 3 and 5. These issues, together with the limited privacy threat model, prevent the otherwise promising empirical contribution from meeting the acceptance threshold.

strengths: The problem is practically relevant: anonymizing reusable features from frozen video encoders could reduce the cost of privacy-aware video analysis.

The evaluation covers multiple backbones and three utility task families. Table 1 reports substantial reductions in VISPR attribute prediction while largely preserving utility, including with VideoMAE-B and VJEPA-H.

The ablations provide useful evidence for latent consistency: in Table 5, it substantially improves held-out temporal action detection performance. The appendix also investigates architecture, loss weights, computational cost, and precomputed features.
The perceived-gender experiments show improvements in aggregate subgroup accuracy gaps, and the paper explicitly acknowledges limitations of binary gender categorization.
weaknesses: The privacy evaluation does not substantiate the broad anonymization claims. VISPR tests seven attributes on repeated-frame image inputs, whereas deployment concerns real video features. PA-HMDB adds relevant video evidence, but its reported privacy reduction is considerably smaller (69.9 to 62.6 cMAP). There is no systematic evaluation against stronger adaptive attackers or calibration against attribute-prevalence baselines. Moreover, Section 4.1 specifies a linear attacker, while Appendix B specifies a two-layer MLP.

The central information-theoretic justification is unsupported. Maximizing NT-Xent with a fixed similarity function does not establish that mutual information decreases: worsening a contrastive lower bound need not decrease the underlying mutual information. Consequently, claims that the objective destroys shared spatial information or removes all unnecessary spatial information exceed what the objective and experiments demonstrate.

The strongest utility results involve training the anonymizer on all three evaluated task families. Held-out-task results are materially weaker than the claimed general preservation within 1–2%: action-recognition-only training reduces THUMOS14 mAP from 60.82 to 56.45, and Toyota Smarthome training reduces it to 41.30. These results indicate meaningful dependence on training tasks and data distribution.

The comparisons do not adequately isolate the contribution. Prior anonymization methods are compared only with I3D, and the paper lacks matched latent-space baselines such as simple feature perturbation or alternative representation-sanitization objectives. Existing methods are not compared under a clearly matched multitask training setup. The novelty of combining a standard adapter, an inherited contrastive objective, and feature reconstruction is therefore insufficiently established.

Temporal privacy remains unresolved. Gait recognition is evaluated through retrieval without training an adaptive attacker. Removing latent consistency improves the reported privacy metric but also severely damages held-out utility elsewhere, so this experiment does not demonstrate a satisfactory solution for sensitive temporal attributes.

The fairness evidence is preliminary. NTU uses one shortcut action without repeated sampling or uncertainty estimates, and Toyota Smarthome uses aggregate subgroup accuracy gaps despite differing action distributions. Class-conditioned results, stronger debiasing baselines, and variability across protocol constructions are needed to support the broader fairness claims.

Reproducibility and reporting need improvement. Temporal tokenization and pooling within AAM, multitask batch scheduling, and exact bias splits are insufficiently specified. Results lack uncertainty estimates despite several small claimed gains. Unexplained discrepancies include the raw HMDB51 baseline across Tables 3 and 5 and the default VideoMAE-B anomaly result across Tables 1 and 8.

strengths: The practical motivation is compelling: anonymizing stored features from frozen video encoders could reduce the cost of privacy interventions while supporting multiple downstream tasks.

The evaluation covers several backbones and three utility task families. Table 1 shows substantial reductions in measured attribute predictability with small utility losses; VideoMAE-B VISPR cMAP falls from 70.47 to 49.92 while THUMOS14 mAP remains near baseline.

The loss ablations provide useful evidence for latent consistency: in Table 5, it substantially restores unseen temporal action detection performance compared with utility-plus-privacy training alone.
The efficiency experiments and exploratory gender-bias evaluations add practical value, including improvements in disadvantaged-group accuracy in the reported protocols.
weaknesses: The central privacy claim exceeds the evidence. Maximizing a fixed cosine-based NT-Xent loss does not establish that mutual information or sensitive information has been destroyed; it can change representation geometry without eliminating recoverable attributes. No derivation supports the claimed removal of all nonessential spatial information.

Privacy evaluation is insufficiently adversarial. Most evidence comes from seven VISPR attributes on repeated-image clips, with limited evaluation on actual videos. Section 4.1 specifies a linear attacker, whereas Appendix B specifies a two-layer MLP. Stronger adaptive attackers, temporal aggregation attacks, per-attribute results, and prevalence-based reference scores are needed to establish the extent of protection. PA-HMDB provides useful additional evidence, but its cMAP reduction is only 69.9 to 62.6.

Comparisons do not isolate the proposed contribution adequately. Prior anonymization methods are compared primarily on I3D, and there are no matched latent-space baselines such as feature perturbation, dimensionality reduction, or adaptations of prior privacy objectives using the same frozen encoder, adapter, and utility training. Consequently, gains cannot clearly be attributed to the proposed objective rather than the change in intervention space and training setup.

Generalization claims are overstated. The strongest Table 1 results train on all three utility task families. Held-out-task performance can deteriorate substantially: Table 3 reports THUMOS14 mAP falling from 60.82 to 41.30 after Toyota Smarthome training, and Table 12 reports drops of 6–9 points for InternVideo-H. These results do not support uniformly retaining utility within 1–2%.

Technical novelty is incompletely established. The method combines a standard attention adapter, an adaptation of an existing self-supervised privacy objective, multitask losses, and feature reconstruction regularization. Broader positioning against representation sanitization and invariant representation learning is needed to substantiate the claimed novel formulation.

Reproducibility and uncertainty reporting need improvement. Attention tokenization and temporal feature organization are unclear, dataset split and bias-protocol details are incomplete, and repeated-run variability is absent. The fairness experiments use one shortcut action and no dedicated debiasing baselines, so reduced aggregate gender accuracy gaps provide limited evidence for broader fairness claims.

strengths: The problem is practically relevant: anonymizing stored video embeddings while keeping the encoder frozen could reduce training and feature-extraction costs and support multiple downstream applications.

The evaluation covers several backbones and diverse tasks, including action recognition, temporal localization, anomaly detection, and retrieval. Table 1 shows substantial reductions in VISPR attribute-prediction performance with small utility losses.

The loss ablations provide useful evidence that latent consistency improves transfer to unseen tasks. The supplementary architecture, training-data, and efficiency experiments strengthen the empirical investigation.
The paper evaluates video-level sensitive attributes, includes inversion attacks, and explicitly acknowledges white-box vulnerability and limitations of binary perceived-gender labels.
weaknesses: The central privacy claim exceeds the evidence. In Table 8, white-box inversion restores attribute cMAP from 70.5 to 73.7 on VP-HMDB51, close to the raw-feature value of 76.4; VP-UCF101 shows similar recovery. Calling white-box access unrealistic is insufficient for a framework intended to support feature sharing. The near-chance black-box inversion result also does not establish strong privacy: a classifier trained directly on anonymized embeddings already achieves substantially higher attribute-prediction performance. The threat model needs explicit justification and stronger adaptive attacker evaluation.

The adapter architecture is inconsistent with the claimed temporal-attention mechanism. Sections 3.1 and B.1 explicitly state that AAM receives a single globally pooled clip embedding. Standard self-attention over one token has a constant attention weight and cannot attend across temporal positions. The paper does not specify any alternative tokenization that resolves this issue, undermining both reproducibility and the explanation for the attention adapter's advantage over MLPs.

The information-theoretic interpretation of the privacy objective is unsupported. Maximizing a fixed NT-Xent loss can make its similarity-based discrimination fail without removing mutual information or sensitive attributes recoverable by another predictor. Reversing a contrastive objective does not establish mutual-information minimization. Claims that the method destroys all unnecessary spatial information require substantially stronger evidence.

The headline privacy and generalization claims are overstated. The 35.5% relative privacy reduction applies to I3D on static-image VISPR; the other Table 1 backbones achieve about 29%, while video-level attribute cMAP falls by only about six absolute points in Table 2 and remains well above chance. Near-baseline utility in Table 1 includes training on the evaluated task types. Held-out-task results are weaker: Table 4 includes THUMOS14 drops from 60.82 to 52.18 or 41.30, depending on the training dataset.

Novelty and comparative evaluation are insufficiently established. The method combines latent adapters, a reversed contrastive objective inherited conceptually from prior anonymization work, multitask training, and an L2 feature-consistency penalty. Positioning concentrates on pixel-level video anonymization without adequately addressing broader representation sanitization and adversarial feature learning. Comparisons against prior anonymization methods are largely restricted to I3D; stronger matched latent-space baselines and comparative privacy–utility curves are needed.

The reconstruction evidence does not isolate a benefit from anonymization. Figure 4 shows that the decoder already fails to recover meaningful content from raw CLS embeddings. Failure on anonymized CLS embeddings therefore offers limited additional evidence. Applying the adapter to patch tokens also differs from its stated training and deployment setting, and the qualitative example does not establish general reconstruction resistance.

The fairness conclusions and small utility differences lack statistical support. No repeated-run uncertainty is reported, and the NTU experiment uses one selected shortcut action without demonstrating robustness across choices. Aggregate gender accuracy gaps, particularly on naturally imbalanced Toyota Smarthome, can reflect differing action distributions and do not alone establish reduced reliance on gender. Exact split manifests, class-conditioned or worst-group metrics, and comparisons with established debiasing methods would make these conclusions more convincing.

strengths: The deployment setting is useful: anonymizing stored video embeddings while keeping a large pretrained encoder frozen could substantially reduce training and feature-extraction costs.

Evaluation covers multiple backbones and downstream tasks, including action recognition, temporal action detection, anomaly detection, and retrieval. Table 1 reports a promising empirical tradeoff: VideoMAE-B privacy cMAP decreases from 70.47 to 49.92 while utility changes are small.

The task-subset and loss ablations provide meaningful evidence that latent consistency helps preserve unseen-task performance. The paper also investigates temporal attributes, inversion attacks, computational efficiency, and demographic performance gaps.
weaknesses: The claimed privacy mechanism is not established. Maximizing NT-Xent does not generally minimize mutual information: weakening a contrastive lower bound does not establish that the underlying mutual information decreases. Reduced cosine similarity can coexist with recoverable sensitive information. Consequently, claims that the objective destroys shared spatial information or removes all unnecessary spatial information substantially exceed the justification provided.

There is a central architectural inconsistency. Section 3.1 explicitly states that AAM operates on a single global clip embedding, yet the method attributes its advantages to self-attention across the temporal dimension. Standard self-attention over one token has a constant attention weight and cannot perform temporal token selection. The paper needs exact tensor shapes and an explanation of the attention axis; the current description does not support its architectural rationale.

The attack results substantially limit the privacy claim. In Table 8, white-box inversion restores privacy cMAP to 73.7 versus 76.4 on raw VP-HMDB51 features, and 72.6 versus 75.9 on VP-UCF101. Dismissing white-box access as typically unrealistic is insufficient for a shareable adapter. Moreover, the black-box inversion attack performs worse than directly classifying anonymized features, so its near-chance result does not establish strong protection. Stronger adaptive classifiers, attack-budget sweeps, and a clearly bounded threat model are needed.

The headline privacy reduction is not representative of the video-level evaluations. Table 2 reduces cMAP by only 5.9 and 6.3 percentage points, leaving substantial performance above the reported chance levels. The roughly 35% relative reduction occurs for I3D on static VISPR inputs; VideoMAE-B and V-JEPA achieve approximately 29% there. Average cMAP reduction should not be equated with removal of sensitive information, especially without per-attribute results.

Comparisons do not sufficiently isolate the contribution. Table 1 compares prior anonymization methods only on I3D, while larger-backbone experiments largely compare against raw features. Missing matched latent-space baselines—such as feature noise, dimensionality reduction, supervised adversarial sanitization across the full task suite, or an adapted prior self-supervised objective—make it difficult to distinguish the benefit of the formulation from the specific proposed method. Positioning against broader representation-sanitization work is also limited.

Unseen-task generalization is useful but overstated. In Table 4, HMDB51-trained anonymization reduces THUMOS14 mAP from 60.82 to 56.50; Toyota-trained anonymization reduces it to 41.30 and UCF-Crime AUC from 85.79 to 74.92. Table 15 also shows substantial temporal-detection drops for large models. These results do not support a general claim of retaining utility within 1–2% across tasks.

Several supporting conclusions lack sufficient validation. Reconstruction from raw CLS tokens already fails, so Figure 4 provides limited evidence of additional protection from anonymization. Fairness evaluation reports aggregate gender gaps without established debiasing baselines, action-conditioned analysis, or uncertainty estimates. Reproducibility is further weakened by missing attack hyperparameters and inconsistent reported values, including UCF-Crime AUC of 85.08 in Table 1 versus 84.33 for the apparently corresponding three-layer adapter in Table 10.

strengths: The problem is practically relevant: sanitizing cached video embeddings while keeping a large encoder frozen could reduce the cost of privacy-aware video analysis.

Evaluation spans multiple backbones and several downstream tasks, including action recognition, temporal action detection, anomaly detection, and retrieval. Table 1 demonstrates a promising empirical tradeoff: VideoMAE-B VISPR cMAP decreases from 70.47 to 49.92 while utility metrics remain close to baseline.

The loss ablations provide useful evidence for latent consistency regularization. In Table 6, it substantially improves held-out temporal detection performance compared with utility and privacy objectives alone.
The manuscript includes architecture, efficiency, gait-recognition, inversion-attack, and perceived-gender-bias experiments, and explicitly acknowledges failure against white-box inversion.
weaknesses: The central privacy mechanism is not technically established. Maximizing NT-Xent with a fixed similarity function does not establish that mutual information decreases: weakening a contrastive lower bound does not imply reducing the underlying information. Consequently, statements that the method destroys shared information or removes all unnecessary spatial information exceed the evidence.

The attack results undermine the broad anonymization claims. White-box inversion restores private-attribute cMAP to 73.7 versus 76.4 originally on VP-HMDB51, and 72.6 versus 75.9 on VP-UCF101. Dismissing this access model as typically unrealistic is insufficient without a clearly justified deployment threat model. Moreover, black-box inversion performs worse than directly classifying anonymized features, so its near-chance results do not establish strong attack resistance. Evaluation needs stronger, varied adaptive attribute predictors beyond the specified two-layer MLP.

The architectural explanation is inconsistent with the stated input. Section 3.1 and Appendix B specify that AAM receives a single globally pooled clip embedding. Standard self-attention over one token has a trivial attention weight and cannot explicitly attend across temporal positions. The claimed temporal reasoning advantage and attention-head ablations therefore require precise tensor shapes and a corrected explanation.

Comparisons do not sufficiently isolate the contribution of the proposed objectives from the benefit of moving anonymization into feature space. Most baselines are pixel-level methods, with comparative results concentrated on I3D. Table 2 includes a useful supervised latent variant, but broader comparisons against feature-space adversarial sanitization and simple perturbation or projection baselines at matched utility are missing. Positioning against privacy-preserving representation learning is also limited.

Generalization and privacy improvements are overstated. The headline 35% privacy reduction is demonstrated on static-image VISPR with I3D; video privacy cMAP falls only from 76.4 to 70.5 and 75.9 to 69.6. Held-out utility losses can also be substantial: action-only training reduces THUMOS14 mAP from 60.82 to 56.45, while Toyota Smarthome training reduces it to 41.30. These results support a conditional tradeoff rather than uniformly near-baseline generalization.

Statistical and reproducibility support is incomplete. Results lack repeated-run uncertainty, which matters particularly for the small utility and fairness improvements. The bias experiments lack competing debiasing baselines and class-conditional analysis to distinguish demographic disparity from action-distribution effects. Attack optimization details and exact bias-split construction are insufficiently specified for confident replication.
